fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Spagyrics anyone can do at home", "body": "Benjamin Balderson opens by insisting that lab alchemy starts cheap and simple, not with rare equipment. He points to his friend Homie Romy, who runs the whole process with a thrift store copper teapot, a hardware store coil and a little pump, the same basic still a moonshiner in Appalachia would recognize. The only real requirement is an enclosed system that can vaporize a liquid and then cool that vapor back into fluid. Chance Garton frames the episode around this practical entry point, wanting listeners who love the philosophy of nature to finally get their feet off the ground."}, {"title": "Separating oil, salt and body", "body": "The core walkthrough is a separation. Balderson soaks plant material in high proof alcohol, ideally Everclear or an alcohol fermented from the same plant, because the higher the percentage the more solvent it is. That pulls the oil out. The leftover mush goes into a cast iron pot over extreme flame for calcination, turning black, then gray, then finally a white powder like baby powder. Distilled water dissolves the mineral salts out of that ash, gets filtered through coffee filters until clear, and then evaporates away, leaving a small pile of the plant's own cell salts."}, {"title": "Why he refuses to add the alcohol back", "body": "Here Balderson breaks with most alchemists, and says he rarely talks about it. Many treat the fermented alcohol as the spirit of the plant and mix it back in as a tincture. He does not. For him alcohol is the negative side of mercury, the side that takes and strips and spikes the cell open. He asks Chance Garton to apply as above so below, pointing out that in metal work the solvent is hydrochloric and sulfuric acid, and nobody would leave acid in something you eat. So why leave the solvent in the plant medicine."}, {"title": "Mercury as the messenger between two halves", "body": "Mercury, in this telling, is simply whatever acts as solvent at a given level, and its identity keeps changing step by step. Water, alcohol, acid and finally the oil itself all take that role. Balderson describes an electron and an ion as one particle split in two with a field between them, and says only through the mercurial fluid can those halves rejoin. Chance Garton connects that to Dionysus and Jesus as lords of wine, to Castor and Pollux, and to mercury as the messenger who carries money, messages and souls from one point to another."}, {"title": "The salt is where memory is kept", "body": "The alchemical marriage is what makes the episode philosophical. Balderson puts the salt back into the oil with no solvent, warms it gently, and waits for the graininess to clear the way sugar dissolves into butter. The yellow sulfur life inside the oil then enlivens the salt, and the two coagulate into the stone. Because the salt now evaporates with the oil, the marriage holds. From that he argues that when a person dies and separates from their salt they lose memory, since salt is the stable side, the wisdom side, and reincarnation follows from that break."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Odin's favorite wizard, Benjamin Balderson, returns to InnerVerse to give us the 101 course on the process of laboratory alchemy. In this episode you'll learn the steps of alchemy from distillation to chemical wedding, the logic of alcohol-free tinctures, the alchemical fractal in nature, and how this study may impact the course of our after-life journey.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension we dive deep into how nature alchemizes on all scales, performing the great work on ourselves, the meaning behind quickening synchronicity, how alchemy relates to astrotheology, alchenomics of currency, ancestors, and the two I AMs.
